description: Bear the builder stacks word blocks on a sentence beam; Robo and Frog learn that a sentence is a whole idea with a capital start, finger spaces and an end mark (period, question mark, exclamation mark), fix broken sentences and take a builder quiz.

youtube.title: Capital Letters and Punctuation for Kids! Sentence Builders | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Bear the builder stacks word blocks on a beam, but the sentence wobbles, words squash together and Frog can't stop reading! Kids learn the sentence rules: a sentence tells a whole idea (who and what they do), starts with a capital letter, has finger spaces between words and ends with a mark: a period for telling, a question mark for asking and an exclamation mark for a strong feeling. Then the Fix-it crew repairs broken sentences and everyone takes the builder quiz.

For first graders (CCSS L.1.2.a, L.1.2.b, L.1.1.j).

Try at home: with a grown-up, write words on paper strips and build a sentence on the floor: a capital start, a finger space between words and an end mark. Swap the end mark and read it again! Use safety scissors, or tear the strips.

do.text: Sentence Builders
Up go the word blocks! Building a sentence!
I'll read it! the sun is hot and... and... and...
I can't stop! Where does it end?
This sentence needs builders. Let's learn the rules!
The red ball.
Hmm. What does the red ball do?
It doesn't say! It isn't finished.
The red ball rolls.
Who? The red ball.
What does it do? It rolls.
Who, and what they do. That's a whole idea!
a whole idea
A sentence tells a whole idea!
frogs can hop. Look at the start.
A small f can't hold the start. The beam tips!
Rule one. Start with a capital letter!
Big F. Now the beam is steady!
Rule one: a capital.
I see Bear. Names get capitals too!
That's me! Big B for Bear.
Let me read this one. Thesunishot!
Thesunishot? What's a thesunishot?
The words are squashed together. They need spaces!
The sun is hot. Now each word has its own space.
Hold up one finger. That's a finger space!
finger space
Long ago, some books had no spaces at all!
Rule two: spaces.
Frog hops. Frog, read it as you hop!
Frog hops... and hops... and hops!
Whoa! Nothing stopped me. I hopped right off!
A sentence needs a stopper at the end.
The period! Try again, Frog.
Frog hops. Stop! The period stopped me!
A period ends a telling sentence.
period
In many places, a period is called a full stop.
Big start, spaces, stop!
Big start! Space, space! STOP!
Look outside. Rain! One sentence, three end marks.
It is raining.
A period. That's a telling sentence.
telling
What end mark comes next? It asks.
Is it raining?
A question mark. My voice goes up, for asking.
asking
Question marks are more than a thousand years old!
It is raining!
Rain! Puddles! I love it!
An exclamation mark shows a strong feeling.
strong feeling
Draw a question mark in the air. Now jump for the exclamation mark!
Read along with me. Listen to my voice change.
It is raining.
Is it raining?
It is raining!
Fix-it crew! This sentence is missing parts.
my hat is red. What's missing?
A capital at the start! And a stopper!
My hat is red.
Next one. Whereisthedrum?
Squashed! It needs finger spaces!
Where is the drum?
I built this one. Do you like pizza.
Robo, it asks something. It needs a question mark!
Oops! Do you like pizza?
Quiz time! Which one is right?
Question 1
The second one! It has a capital T.
Question two. What mark ends this one?
Question 2
A question mark! Can you swim?
Question three. We won! We are so excited.
Question 3
An exclamation mark! We won!
Question four. How many words? Count them.
Question 4
Four words: I, like, my, hat.
Last one. The tall tree. Is that a whole sentence?
Question 5
No! It doesn't say what the tree does.
The tall tree sways. Frog, will you finish it?
Stop! I love a stopper!
We built a sentence!
Master builders!
A whole idea, a capital, spaces, and an end mark.
Big start! Space, space! Stop!
Telling. Asking? WOW!
Big start, space, stop! Bye, builders!
